rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds while promoting elution of all 10 within the acquisition window. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent optimization of gradient range, duration, and temperature.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin is preserved. Keep temperature and endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.
Keep the fast gradient and increase temperature to test whether temperature-dependent selectivity separates the crowded middle peaks. This also should preserve the low retention-time penalty.

Test lower-temperature selectivity with the same fast gradient, since heating improved one crowded region but created another limiting pair. This brackets the temperature response while retaining a short analysis time.
Slightly lengthen the gradient at the best temperature to improve the limiting middle-pair separation. The last peak should remain below eight minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near the maximum-scoring method to increase the resolution margin of the earlier close pair. The last peak is expected near eight minutes, probing whether full resolution and zero time penalty can both be retained.

Probe temperature sensitivity around the maximum-scoring method by lowering temperature five degrees. This tests whether the two closest peak groups can retain adequate resolution with a larger operating margin.

Complete the local temperature bracket around the maximum-scoring method. Higher temperature should shorten retention and improve the later close pair, while testing whether the earlier close pair becomes limiting.

Test a modest increase in starting organic fraction at the best temperature to shorten retention and probe selectivity of the two close middle pairs. Injection 5 already achieves the maximum CRF; this explores whether another maximum-scoring method offers more resolution margin.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the limiting pair from injection 9 while retaining its shorter retention times. This may provide full resolution with more balanced margins than injection 5 and no time penalty.

Reduce gradient steepness one more step to bring the limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The predicted last-peak time is approximately eight minutes, near the zero-penalty boundary.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to explore another route to full resolution within eight minutes. The maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests whether the close-pair resolution margins can be improved without a time penalty.

Explore a much faster gradient at high temperature, which may move the earlier limiting pair through an elution-order reversal and restore separation. The maximum CRF is already secured; this tests for an equally scoring method with substantially shorter retention times.

Preserve injection 5’s gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed gradient. Since all peaks previously eluted before this gradient ends, this method should retain the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Keep the maximum-scoring gradient slope while ending the ramp at a lower organic fraction. All peaks should elute before the gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 8.65 minutes, preserving the observed separation and CRF.

Use a gradient slope between injections 10 and 11 to target both close-pair resolutions above 1.5 with the last peak below eight minutes. This may retain the maximum CRF while balancing resolution and retention-time margins.

Explore higher starting organic fraction at 60 °C to test whether the earlier close pair separates after an elution-order reversal. The maximum CRF is already secured; this probes a distinct selectivity region for a faster, fully resolved alternative.

Increase starting organic fraction to test whether the limiting pair separates further in the reversed-order region, while lengthening the gradient to preserve other separations. This explores a faster alternative to the established maximum-scoring methods.

Preserve the maximum-scoring gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the isolated last peak still elutes within eight minutes, retaining CRF 1.000 with a lower final organic fraction.

Injection 19 shows that zero time penalty extends beyond eight minutes. Test a shallower gradient at 10% starting organic to improve the earlier close pair while aiming to preserve the later pair’s resolution and the maximum CRF.

Lengthen injection 12’s gradient to improve its limiting middle-pair resolution while retaining the stronger separation of the later close pair. This tests whether a higher starting organic fraction can provide larger resolution margins without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

Slightly flatten injection 21’s gradient to raise its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The last peak is expected near nine minutes, testing whether improved resolution can still retain the maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 11’s gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 60% organic. All peaks should elute before the gradient endpoint reaches the outlet, retaining its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of 1.58.

Lower the endpoint one step to test whether a shallower gradient increases the earlier close-pair separation while keeping the later pair above 1.5. The last peak should remain near the observed zero-time-penalty region, potentially preserving the maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a gradient slope between injections 23 and 24, targeting full resolution with the last peak around 8.3 minutes and no time penalty. The campaign has already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000; this final run probes another method expected to retain that score.
